title: Double-counting and shared objects
transcript: A double-counting argument counts the same thing from two viewpoints. Both totals must describe the same physical objects or links. If every link is reported by its two endpoints, the endpoint total is twice the number of links.

AMC Upper Primary practice can use handshakes or matches. Draw one pair to see how many times it appears when people report their own totals. In a Mawa style counting argument, name exactly what the two calculations count. A participant-room booking differs from an individual participant.
Five students each shake hands with every other student once. How many handshakes take place? Imagine asking each student how many handshakes they took part in.
Each student reports four handshakes. The reports add to twenty. A handshake is reported by both students in the pair. Divide by two to find ten different handshakes.

At a festival, each of six rooms schedules eight different helpers. Each helper has a booking in exactly three distinct rooms. Find the total number of helpers. A booking is one helper assigned to one room.
By rooms there are forty-eight total bookings. Counting by helpers gives three bookings for every helper. Divide the booking total by three. This gives sixteen individual helpers.

In a tournament of ten players each pair can play at most once. Exactly four players each play against everyone else. Each of the other six players misses exactly one opponent. How many matches are played?
The first group each reports nine matches, and the second group each reports eight matches. The reports add to eighty-four. Each played match has two players, so the actual count is forty-two.

Check from the full schedule of forty-five matches. The six missed-opponent reports come in pairs, giving three matches that fell through. The difference is forty-two, agreeing with the endpoint count.

In a two-person match, each report identifies one endpoint. A total of personal match counts records twice as many entries as actual matches. Room bookings and helpers are different units. Read whether the question asks for assignments or the number of people who hold those assignments.

Write what one object is, such as a match or a helper-room booking. Then write down each viewpoint. Work out how many times your calculation reports one object. Use that ratio to put the answer in the units requested.
